\chapter{Milk, Cheese, Juice, and Soup}
\label{ch:russian-milk-cheese-juice-soup}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name milk, cheese, juice and soup in Russian with their genders, ask for any of them politely, and say which are inherited and which are borrowed.}

The chapter closes on \ru{суп}, a French loan that mirrors \ru{кофе}'s story from the opposite direction: the reader produces \ru{молоко}, \ru{сыр}, \ru{сок} and \ru{суп} with their genders, extends Chapter 6's request pattern to all four, and sorts the set into a hand-motion cousin, a taste cousin, an honest dead end, and a shared loanword. It reaches all the way back to Chapter 2 to rescue the naming-question comparison and \ru{я}'s script warning, the last two atoms in the track that nothing had revisited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[malakó]{\ru{молоко} — \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} a cousin down to the hand motion}

\label{lesson:RU-C13-moloko}



\begin{quote}
\emph{\ru{Мать}} and \emph{\ru{отец}} just closed the family — remember \emph{\ru{папа}}'s odd masculine ending on the way past — and now a new chapter, back to the water-coffee-tea-bread drink shelf to add three more words, starting with one whose English cousin shares not just a sound, but the very gesture the word describes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{молоко}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{молоко}} — \emph{malakó} — \textbf{milk}. \textbf{Neuter.}
\end{quote}

Stress on the last syllable, and the two unstressed \textbf{\ru{о}}s both reduce toward \emph{a} — the \emph{akanye} rule from your very first lessons, doing real work here: \emph{ma-la-KÓ}, not \emph{mo-lo-KO}. The \textbf{-\ru{о}} ending gives the third gender, same row as \emph{\ru{ухо}} and \emph{\ru{сердце}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{молоко}} continues Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}melǵ-}, \textquotedblleft{}to rub, to stroke, to milk\textquotedblright{} — a root that names the \emph{motion of the hand}, not the liquid itself, exactly the way English \textbf{milk} does too: English \textbf{milk}, German \textbf{Milch}, Latin \textbf{mulgeō} (\textquotedblleft{}I milk,\textquotedblright{} $\to$ the rare English \emph{emulsion} relative), and Greek \textbf{amélgō} all continue the same word. Say \emph{\ru{молоко}, milk, Milch, mulgeō} together and every one of them still carries the memory of a hand closing around an udder.

One honest complication: some etymologists treat the Slavic word as a \textbf{borrowing} from early Germanic rather than an independent inheritance from the same PIE root — the same kind of hedge this book already gave \emph{\ru{думать}} and its link to \textbf{doom}. Either way, \emph{\ru{молоко}} and \emph{milk} share the same ultimate ancestor; the only open question is how directly.

Ask for it the way you already know:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Молоко}, \ru{пожалуйста}.} — \emph{malakó, pazhálusta} — \textbf{Milk, please.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{молоко}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ma-la-KÓ}, neuter, both \ru{о}'s reduced
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{молоко}, milk, Milch, mulgeō\textquotedblright{} — the hand's motion, four languages
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{Молоко}, \ru{пожалуйста}.\textquotedblright{} — the request pattern, holding steady
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Молоко}} — \textbf{neuter}.) What did its PIE root originally describe — the liquid, or something else? (\textbf{The hand motion of milking.}) Name two Germanic cousins. (\textbf{Milk, Milch.}) Ask for milk politely. (\textbf{\ru{Молоко}, \ru{пожалуйста}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[syr]{\ru{сыр} — \textquotedblleft{}cheese,\textquotedblright{} which is really just an old word for \textquotedblleft{}sour\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:RU-C13-syr}



\begin{quote}
Bread's natural partner, finally on the table — and a word whose Russian double life gives away exactly how it got its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{сыр}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{сыр}} — \emph{syr} — \textbf{cheese}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

One syllable, consonant-final — the regular rule again, no exception. Say it with the vowel \emph{\ru{ты}} already made you practise: drawn back in the throat, not the \emph{ee} of \emph{\ru{и}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{сыр}} is, historically, the same word as \textbf{\ru{сырой}}, \textquotedblleft{}raw, damp, uncooked\textquotedblright{} — cheese named not for what it becomes, but for the state its milk was in on the way there. Both continue a Proto-Indo-European root for \textquotedblleft{}sour, damp,\textquotedblright{} and the family shows up right on English's own doorstep: \textbf{English \emph{sour}} (Old English \emph{sūr}, from the same Germanic branch), \textbf{Old Norse \emph{súrr}}, \textbf{Old High German \emph{sûr}}. Say \emph{\ru{сырой}, sour, súrr, sûr} and you are hearing one old idea of \textquotedblleft{}gone tart\textquotedblright{} spread across the whole Germanic half of the family, with Russian's \emph{\ru{сыр}} sitting one short step away from all of it.

That gives you the chapter's drink-and-bread shelf a genuine internal logic: \textbf{\ru{молоко}} was named for the \emph{hand} that made it; \textbf{\ru{сыр}} is named for the \emph{taste} milk takes on before it becomes food at all.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Сыр}, \ru{пожалуйста}.} — \emph{syr, pazhálusta} — \textbf{Cheese, please.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сыр}\textquotedblright{} — masculine, the pulled-back \ru{ы}
  \item the double life — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сыр} and \ru{сырой}, one root\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сырой}, sour, súrr, sûr\textquotedblright{} — Slavic and Germanic, side by side
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{Сыр}, \ru{пожалуйста}. \ru{Хлеб}, \ru{пожалуйста}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{syr, pazhálusta; khleb, pazhálusta}) — cheese and bread, the request pattern's pair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}cheese,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Сыр}} — \textbf{masculine}.) What Russian adjective does \emph{\ru{сыр}} secretly share its root with, and what does it mean? (\textbf{\ru{Сырой}}, \textquotedblleft{}raw, damp.\textquotedblright{}) Name its English cousin. (\textbf{Sour.}) Ask for it politely. (\textbf{\ru{Сыр}, \ru{пожалуйста}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sok]{\ru{сок} — \textquotedblleft{}juice,\textquotedblright{} ancient and untranslatable into English cousins}

\label{lesson:RU-C13-sok}



\begin{quote}
The third drink on this chapter's shelf — and, like \emph{\ru{скорого}} and \emph{\ru{встречи}} before it, a root old enough to reconstruct and still without a single confirmed English relative.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{сок}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{сок}} — \emph{sok} — \textbf{juice}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

One syllable, consonant-final, the regular rule holding for the third lesson running. Every letter you have owned for a long time now.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{сок}} reconstructs cleanly to Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*sok\textsuperscript{w}ós}, by way of Proto-Balto-Slavic \textbf{*sakás} — this is not a shaky guess the way \emph{\ru{рот}}'s root was, but a solid reconstruction with real evidence behind it. What it does \textbf{not} have is a surviving cousin anywhere in English or the rest of Germanic: the trail is well documented all the way back, and then simply stops before it reaches the language you already speak.

That is worth holding next to \emph{\ru{молоко}} and \emph{\ru{сыр}}, the two words either side of it on this shelf: three drinks, three different outcomes. \emph{\ru{Молоко}} connects to English down to the hand motion. \emph{\ru{Сыр}} connects through a Germanic side door, by way of \emph{sour}. \emph{\ru{Сок}} connects to nothing at all — and all three are equally real, equally ancient Russian.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Сок}, \ru{пожалуйста}.} — \emph{sok, pazhálusta} — \textbf{Juice, please.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{сок}\textquotedblright{} — masculine, one syllable
  \item the honest gap — \textquotedblleft{}*sok\textsuperscript{w}ós, well attested, no English cousin\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three-way contrast — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{молоко}, \ru{сыр}, \ru{сок} — hand motion, sourness, and nothing at all\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{Сок}, \ru{пожалуйста}.\textquotedblright{} — juice, please
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}juice,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Сок}} — \textbf{masculine}.) Does it have a confirmed English cousin? (\textbf{No} — a solid PIE root, but no surviving Germanic descendant.) Which of this chapter's three drink words connects to English through a hand motion, and which through a taste? (\textbf{\ru{Молоко}} through milking; \textbf{\ru{сыр}} through \emph{sour}.) Ask for juice politely. (\textbf{\ru{Сок}, \ru{пожалуйста}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sup]{\ru{суп} — \textquotedblleft{}soup,\textquotedblright{} the same French word English also borrowed}

\label{lesson:RU-C13-sup}



\begin{quote}
The last word on this chapter's table — and, like \emph{\ru{кофе}} before it, a loanword rather than an inheritance, which makes it the perfect word to close on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — \ru{суп}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{суп}} — \emph{sup} — \textbf{soup}. \textbf{Masculine.}
\end{quote}

One syllable, consonant-final, the regular rule holding one last time. Every letter is one you have owned for a long time now.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{суп}} is a straight loan from \textbf{French \emph{soupe}}, part of the flood of French vocabulary that entered Russian aristocratic life in the 1700s — the same century, and nearly the same social world, that gave \emph{\ru{кофе}} its own sea route into the language. Chase \emph{soupe} back further and it comes from Late Latin \textbf{suppa}, \textquotedblleft{}bread soaked in broth.\textquotedblright{}

Here is what makes \emph{\ru{суп}} different from everything else on this shelf: \textbf{English \emph{soup} took the identical French word}, by a separate crossing, centuries apart from Russian's own borrowing. So \emph{\ru{суп}} and \emph{soup} \textbf{are} related — but by two languages independently reaching for the same French word, not by shared Russian-English ancestry. It mirrors \emph{\ru{кофе}} and \emph{coffee}, which took one Arabic word by two different European doors; here, two languages took the \emph{same} French door, just at different times.

Ask for the whole shelf the way you already know:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{Молоко}, \ru{сыр}, \ru{сок} \ru{и} \ru{суп}, \ru{пожалуйста}.} — \textbf{Milk, cheese, juice and soup, please.}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ru{суп}\textquotedblright{} — masculine, one syllable
  \item the loan — \textquotedblleft{}French soupe, 1700s, same century as \ru{кофе}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the mirror — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{суп}/soup: one French word, two borrowings; \ru{кофе}/coffee: one Arabic word, two doors\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole shelf — \textquotedblleft{}\ru{молоко}, \ru{сыр}, \ru{сок}, \ru{суп}, \ru{пожалуйста}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{malakó, syr, sok, sup, pazhálusta})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}soup,\textquotedblright{} with its gender. (\textbf{\ru{Суп}} — \textbf{masculine}.) When did it enter Russian, and from where? (\textbf{The 1700s}, from \textbf{French \emph{soupe}}.) Is \emph{\ru{суп}} related to English \emph{soup} by inheritance or by borrowing? (\textbf{Borrowing} — two separate crossings of the same French word.) Now reach all the way back to the naming-question comparison: which languages ask \textquotedblleft{}how do they call you\textquotedblright{} instead of \textquotedblleft{}what is your name,\textquotedblright{} and what must you never mistake this book's very first letter, \textbf{\ru{я}}, for? (\textbf{Russian and French}, against English's \emph{what}; \textbf{never a mirrored Latin R}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
